questions.text: In this lesson’s stateless request model, why must each request carry its own protocol version and client capabilities?

options.A: So the server can interpret the request without inheriting another request’s context.
options.B: So the client can use its capability declaration as proof of authorization.
options.C: So the server can create a persistent protocol session for each request ID.
options.D: So later requests can omit metadata after the first successful operation.

questions.explanation: Per-request metadata makes each request independently interpretable and prevents context from leaking between clients or requests.

questions.text: In this lesson’s model, a clientInfo object claims name="trusted-admin". How should the server treat that name when authorizing a sensitive operation?

options.A: Grant admin access because clientInfo is carried in request metadata.
options.B: Reuse permissions from the last request with the same displayed name.
options.C: Treat it as display/debugging data and verify authorization separately.
options.D: Accept the name as a credential if its version field is also a string.

questions.explanation: Client identity metadata is self-reported display/debugging data. It is not a security credential.

questions.text: In the supplied dispatcher, a valid tools/list request is followed by another supported-version request with clientCapabilities removed from params._meta. What does the second dispatch return?

options.A: A successful list using capabilities remembered from the first request.
options.B: A JSON-RPC error with code -32602 for the missing capability object.
options.C: A JSON-RPC error with code -32022 for an unsupported version.
options.D: No response, because missing capabilities makes it a notification.

questions.explanation: validate_request requires clientCapabilities to be a dict on each request and returns -32602 when it is absent. The dispatcher does not reuse previous metadata.
